{{RunningHeader|think|6293|thio-arsenic}}{{smaller block|In this development [of scientific ethical notions], religion is a fungous growth on the ethical trunk; gods exist in men alone and are ''thought'' into the world. {{right|''New Princeton Rev.'', I. 152.}}}} {{smaller|'''To think little of, to think nothing of''', to make little or no account of; have little or no hesitation about: as, he ''thinks nothing of'' walking his thirty miles a day. ''To think no more of'' is a quasi-comparative form of ''to think nothing of''.}} {{smaller block|The Western people apparently ''think no more of'' throwing down a railroad, if they want to go anywhere, than a conservative Easterner does of taking an unaccustomed walk across country. {{right|''Harper's Mag.'', LXXVI. 565.}}}} {{smaller|'''To think one's penny silver.''' See ''penny''.—'''To think out.''' (''a'') To gain a clear conception or understanding of, by following a line of thought.}} {{smaller block|Jevons's idea of Identity is very difficult; I can hardly suppose it to be ''thought out''. {{right|''B. Bosanquet'', Mind, XIII. 360.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') To devise; plan; project.}} {{smaller block|It is at least possible that if an attempt to invade England on carefully ''thought-out'' lines were made, the world would be equally surprised by the result. {{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XLIII. 156.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') To solve by process of thought: as, to ''think out'' a chess problem.—'''To think scorn of†.''' See ''scorn''.—'''To think small beer of.''' See ''beer''1.='''Syn. 6.''' To judge, suppose, hold, count, account. See ''conjecture''.}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To exercise the intellect, as in apprehension, judgment, or inference; exercise the cognitive faculties in any way not involving outward observation, or the passive reception of ideas from other minds. {{smaller|In this sense the verb ''think'' is often followed, by ''on'', ''of'', ''about'', etc., with the name of the remote object sought to be understood, recalled, appreciated, or otherwise investigated by the mental process.}} {{smaller block|Nothinge lefte thei vn-tolde that thei cowde ''on thenke''. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 370.}}}} {{smaller block|''Thynke ouer'' thi synnes be-fore donne and ''of'' thi freeltes that thou fallis in ilke day. {{right|''Hampole'', Prose Treatises (E. E. T. S.), p. 36.}}}} {{smaller block|And makith his herte as hard as stoon; Thanne ''thenkith'' he not ''on'' heuen blis. {{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 92.}}}} {{smaller block|How we shall carry ourselves in this business is only to be ''thought upon. Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, i. 1.}} {{smaller block|Muckle ''thought'' the gudewife to hersell, Yet ne'er a word she spak. {{right|''Get up and Bar the Door'' (Child's Ballads, VIII. 127).}}}} {{smaller block|And Peter called to mind the word that Jesus said unto him. . . . And when he ''thought'' thereon, he wept. {{right|Mark xiv. 72.}}}} {{smaller block|As I observed that this truth — I ''think'', hence I am — was so certain and of such evidence that no ground of doubt, however extravagant, could be alleged by the Sceptics capable of shaking it, I concluded that I might, without scruple, accept it as the first principle of the Philosophy of which I was in search. {{right|''Descartes'', Discourse on Method (tr. by Veitch), p. 33.}}}} {{smaller block|Light Sordello rose — to ''think'' now; hitherto He had perceived. {{right|''Browning'', Sordello.}}}} {{smaller block|To ''think'' is pre-eminently to detect similarity amid diversity. {{right|''J. Sully'', Outlines of Psychol., p. 331.}}}} {{smaller block|When scarce aught could give him greater fame, He left the world still ''thinking on'' his name. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 427.}}}} 2. To imagine: followed by ''of'' or ''on''. {{smaller block|And he had also in his Gardyn alle maner of Foules and of Bestes, that ony man myghte ''thenke on'', for to have pley or desport to beholde hem. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 278.}}}} {{smaller block|'Tis, I say, their Misfortune not to have ''Thought of'' an Alphabet. {{right|''Lister'', Journey to Paris, p. 49.}}}} 3. To attend (on); fasten the mind (on): followed by ''of''. {{smaller block|That we can at any moment ''think of'' the same thing which at any former moment we ''thought of'' is the ultimate law of our intellectual constitution. {{right|''W. James'', Prin. of Psychology, II. 290.}}}} 4. To entertain a sentiment or opinion (in a specified way): with ''of'': as, to ''think'' highly ''of'' a person's abilities. {{smaller block|But now I forbear, lest any man should ''think of'' me above that which he seeth me to be. {{right|2 Cor. xii. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|''Think of'' me as you please. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., v. 1. 317.}}}} {{smaller block|Justice she ''thought of'' as a thing that might
Balk some desire of hers. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, III. 104.}}}} 5. To have a (specified) feeling (for); be affected (toward); especially, to have a liking or fondness: followed by ''of''. {{smaller block|Marie Hamilton 's to the kirk gane,
Wi' ribbons in her hair;
The King ''thought'' mair ''o''' Marie Hamilton
Than ony that were there. {{right|''The Queen's Marie'' (Child's Ballads, III. 115).}}}} '''To think good.''' See ''good.''—'''To think long.''' (''a'') To long; yearn: usually followed by ''after'' or ''for''. {{smaller block|''Aftir'' his loue me ''thenkith long'',
For he hath myne ful dere y-bouȝte. {{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 9.}}}} {{smaller block|Have I ''thought long'' to see this morning's face,
And doth it give me such a sight as this? {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iv. 5. 41.}}}} {{smaller block|Ae bit I canno' eat, father, . . .
Till I see my mither and sister dear,
For ''lang'' for them I ''think''. {{right|''Young Akin'' (Child's Ballads, I. 185).}} (''b'') To think the time long; become weary or impatient, especially in waiting for something.}} {{smaller block|But gin ye like to ware the time, then ye How a' the matter stood shall vively see; 'Twill may be keep us baith frae ''thinking lang.'' {{right|''Ross'', Helenore, p. 69. (''Jamieson.'')}}}} {{smaller block|[Obsolete or provincial in both senses.] =Syn. 1. To contemplate, reason.}} '''think1''' (thingk), ''n.'' [< ''think''1, ''v.''] A thinking; thought. {{smaller block|He thinks many a long ''think.'' {{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, VII. 914.}}}} '''think2''' (thingk), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''thinken'', ''thenken'', also assibilated ''thinchen'', ''thunchen'' (pret. ''thuhte'', ''thugte'', ''thougte'', ''thauhte''), < AS. ''thyncan'' = OS. ''thunkian'' = OFries. ''thinka'', ''thinszia'', ''tinsa'' = OHG. ''dunchan'', MHG. ''dunken'', G. ''dünken'' = Icel. ''thykkja'' = Sw. ''tycka'' = Dan. ''tykkes'' = Goth. ''thugkjan'', seem, appear: see ''think''1, with which ''think''2 has been more or less confused.] '''1.''' To seem; appear: with indirect object (dative). [Rare except in ''methinks'', ''methought.''] {{smaller block|If it be wykke, a wonder ''thynketh'' me, Whenne every torment and adversite, That cometh of him, may to me savory ''thynke.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, I. 405.}}}} {{smaller block|Ye ''thenke'' as that ye were in a dreme, and I merveile moche of youre grete wisdome where it is be-come. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 226.}}}} {{smaller block|The beggers craft ''thynkynge'' to them moost good. {{right|''Barclay'', Ship of Fools, I. 303.}}}} {{smaller block|The watchman said, Me ''thinketh'' the running of the foremost is like the running of Ahimaaz. {{right|2 Sam. xviii. 27.}}}} '''2'''†. To seem good. {{smaller block|All his [Priam's] sonnes to sle with sleght of your honde; Thaire riches to robbe, & there rife goodis; And no lede for to lyue, but that hom selfe [''i. e.'', to the Greeks themselves] ''thinke''. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4486.}}}} ¶ '''thinkable''' (thing′ka-bl), ''a.'' [< ''think''1 + ''-able''.] Capable of being thought; cogitable; conceivable. {{smaller block|A general relation becomes ''thinkable'', apart from the many special relations displaying it, only as the faculty of abstraction develops. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Prin. of Psychol., § 488.}}}} '''thinker''' (thing′kėr), ''n.'' [< ''think''1 + ''-er''1.] One who thinks; especially, one who has cultivated or exercised to an unusual extent the powers of thought. {{smaller block|A ''Thinker''; memor. {{right|''Cath. Ang.'', p. 383.}}}} {{smaller block|The Democriticks and Epicureans did indeed suppose all humane cogitations to be caused or produced by the incursion of corporeal atoms upon the ''thinker''. {{right|''Cudworth'', Intellectual System, p. 761.}}}} {{smaller block|He considered himself a ''thinker'', and was certainly of a thoughtful turn, but, with his own path to discover, had perhaps hardly yet reached the point where an educated man begins to think. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, xii.}}}} '''thinking''' (thing′king), ''n.'' [< ME. *''thenking'', ''thenching''; verbal n. of ''think''1, ''v.''] '''1.''' The mental operation performed by one who thinks. {{smaller block|''Thinking'', in the propriety of the English tongue, signifies that sort of operation of the mind about its ideas wherein the mind is active. {{right|''Locke'', Human Understanding, II. ix. 1.}}}} '''2.''' The faculty of thought; the mind. {{smaller block|Has Page any brains? hath he any eyes? hath he any ''thinking?'' {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 2. 31.}}}} '''3.''' That which is thought; a thought, idea, belief, opinion, notion, or the like. {{smaller block|I prithee, speak to me as to thy ''thinkings.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 3. 131.}}}} {{smaller block|The idea of the perpetuity of the Roman Empire entered deeply into the Christian ''thinking'' of the middle ages. {{right|''G. P. Fisher'', Begin. of Christianity, p. 41.}}}} '''thinkingly''' (thing′king-li), ''adv.'' With thought or reflection; consciously; deliberately. '''thinly''' (thin′li), ''adv.'' [< ''thin''1 + ''-ly''2.] In a thin manner; with little thickness or depth; sparsely; slightly; not substantially. {{smaller block|At the unexpected sight of him [his brother], Elidure, himself also then but ''thinly'' accompanied, runns to him with open Arms. {{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., i.}}}} {{smaller block|The West is new, vast, and ''thinly'' peopled. {{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Pittsburg, July, 1833.}}}} {{smaller block|The characters are ''thinly'' sketched, the situations at once forced and conventional. {{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XXIV. 536.}}}} '''thinner''' (thin′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''thin''1 + ''-er''1.] One who or that which thins. '''thinness''' (thin′nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''thynnesse'', < AS. ''thynnys'', < ''thynne'', thin: see ''thin''1 and ''-ness.''] The state or property of being thin. {{smaller block|Like those toys Of glassy bubbles, which the gamesome boys Stretch to so nice a ''thinness'' through a quill. {{right|''Donne'', Progress of the Soul, xii.}}}} '''thinnify''' (thin′i-fī), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''thinnified'', ppr. ''thinnifying''. [< ''thin''1 + ''-i-fy.''] To make thin. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The heart doth in its left side ventricle so ''thinnify'' the blood that it thereby obtains the name of spiritual. {{right|''Urquhart'', tr. of Rabelais, iii. 4.}}}} '''thinnish''' (thin′ish), ''a.'' [< ''thin''1 + ''-ish''1.] Somewhat thin. '''Thinocoridæ''' (thin-ọ̄-kor′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Thinocorus'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of limicoline and somewhat charadriomorphic birds of South America, represented by the genera ''Thinocorus'' and ''Attagis''. {{smaller|Their nearest relatives are the sheathbills, with which they have been combined in the family ''Chionididæ''. The palatal structure is peculiar in the broadly rounded vomer, the form and connections of which recall the ægithognathous palate; there are no basipterygoids; the nasals are schizorhinal; superorbital fossæ are present; the carotids are two in number; and the ambiens, femorocaudal, semitendinosus, and their accessories are present. In general outward appearance these birds resemble quails or partridges, and they were formerly considered to be gallinaceous rather than limicoline. They nest on the ground, and lay colored eggs. There are two or three species of each of the genera, of southern parts of the continent, extending into the tropics only in elevated regions. The birds have been singularly called ''tringoid grouse.''}} [[File:century v08 p0097 c3f1.png|center|129px]] {{c|Palate of ''Thinocorus rumicivorus'', one of the ''Thinocoridæ''. (One and a half times natural size.) ''px'', premaxillary; ''mxp'', maxillopalatine; ''vo'', broad vomer, rounded off in front; ''m'', malar; ''pl'', palatal; ''pt'', pterygoid.}} '''thinocorine''' (thī-nok′ọ̄-rin), ''a.'' Characteristic of or pertaining to the ''Thinocoridæ. Stand. Nat. Hist.'', II. 92. '''Thinocorus''' (thī-nok′ọ̄-rus), ''n.'' [NL. (Eschscholtz, 1829), also ''Tinochorus'' (Lesson, 1830), also ''Thinochorus'' (Agassiz, 1846), also ''Thynochorus, Thinocoris;'' prop. *''Thinocorys'', < Gr. θίς (θιν-), the shore, + κόρυς, the crested lark.] The leading genus of ''Thinocoridæ;'' the lark-plovers, as ''T. rumicivorus'', the gachita, of the Argentine Republic, Chili, and other southerly parts of the Neotropical region. {{smaller|This singular bird is common on dry open plains, in flocks. On the ground it resembles a quail, but its flight is more like that of a snipe. It nests on the ground, and lays pale stone-gray eggs heavily marked with light and dark chocolate-brown spots. Other species are described, as ''T. ingæ'', but they are all much alike. The genus is also called ''Ocypetes'' (or ''Oxypetes'') and ''Itys''.}} [[File:century v08 p0097 c3f2.png|center|325px]] {{c|Lark-plover (''Thinocorus ingæ'').}} '''thinolite''' (thin′ō-līt), ''n.'' [< Gr. θίς (θιν-), shore, + λίθος, stone.] A pseudomorphous tufa-like deposit of calcium carbonate, crystalline in form. {{smaller|It is found in great quantities on the shores of Pyramid Lake, Nevada, and at other points within the area of the great Quaternary lake called Lake Lahontan. Its original character is as yet uncertain.}} '''thin-skinned''' (thin′skind), ''a.'' 1. Having a thin skin; hence, unduly sensitive; easily offended; irritable. {{smaller block|Ring's vanity was very ''thin-skinned'', his selfishness easily wounded. {{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, iv.}}}} 2. Having merely a thin superstratum of good soil: said of land. ''Halliwell.'' '''thin-skinnedness''' (thin′skind-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being thin-skinned; oversensitiveness. {{smaller block|This too great susceptibility, or ''thinskinnedness'', as it has been called, is not confined to us. {{right|''L. Cass'', France, its King, etc. (ed. 1841), p. 51.}}}} '''thio-acid''' (thī-ō-as′id), ''n.'' [< Gr. θεῖον, sulphur, + E. ''acid''.] A designation somewhat loosely applied to certain acids derived from others by the substitution of sulphur for oxygen, generally but not always in the hydroxyl group. '''thio-arsenic''' (thī-ō-är′se-nik), ''a.'' [< Gr. θεῖον, sulphur, + ἀρσενικόν, arsenic.] Containing sulphur and arsenic: applied only to certain arsenic acids (see below).—{{smaller|'''Thio-arsenic acid''', an arsenic acid in which sulphur may be regarded as substituted for oxygen. There are three of these acids, not known in the free state, but having well-defined salts. Their formulæ are H4As2S7, H2AsS3, H3AsS4.}}
